reason: I'll strengthen the bones first; the picture shows spaces for mineral in the living framework.
expectation: I expect the mineral to make the bones harder and more resistant to compression.

alternatives.reason: Building the front muscle also fits a goal, but I chose to strengthen the bones first.

effect: The bones are strengthened while the joint stays movable; now I need to build the muscles.
reaction: It was helpful to see that mineral hardens the bone without hardening the joint.
reason: I'll build the front muscle first; its tendons show where the muscle belongs.
expectation: I expect muscle cells to form a muscle between the front attachments, though I'm not sure exactly how.

alternatives.reason: The back muscle also needs building, but either side seems reasonable to start with.

effect: The front cells formed the biceps, which pulls to bend the elbow; the back side still needs a muscle.
reaction: The arrows made the connection between the muscle's position and bending clear.
reason: I'll place muscle cells at the back attachments to build the other muscle; it's the only offered gameplay action.
expectation: I expect a muscle to form behind the elbow and pull it in the opposite direction.

effect: The triceps completes the opposite side: the same kind of muscle cells can straighten the elbow because of where they attach.
reaction: The matching arrows made the contrast with the biceps clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: Building the two muscles was most worthwhile because their positions explained how pulling can bend or straighten the elbow.

leastWorthwhile.text: Placing the second muscle felt somewhat repetitive, though the opposite movement made the comparison useful.

surprise.text: I hadn't expected the same kind of muscle cells to produce opposite movements just because of their attachments.

arbitrary.text: Nothing felt particularly arbitrary: the mineral had visible spaces to fill, and the tendon attachments showed where muscles belonged.

continue.text: Yes, I'd try another chapter: seeing how the same pulling cells make opposite movements made me curious about other body systems.
